title: Monte Carlo Methods
oneLiner: Learn how good situations and choices are by playing to the end many times and averaging what actually happened, with no model of the world needed.

what.html:
Monte Carlo (MC) means estimating something by averaging random samples. In RL: to find out how good a state is, play many episodes, write down the total reward that followed each visit to that state, and average. No rulebook, no probabilities; just outcomes.

Everyday versionA café owner wants to know how good Table 7 is for tips. She has no formula, so she records the tip every time someone sits there and averages over a few hundred visits.

why.html:
• Most real problems have no known model, but you can play them or simulate them.
  • Averages of real outcomes aren't thrown off by wrong guesses about other states.
  • It's the basis of game-tree search and of policy-gradient methods later.

how.title: Sample and average
how.html: Throw random darts to estimate π: the share landing inside a circle tells you its area. RL does the same with returns: run the policy, collect totals, average them.

how.title: First visit or every visit
how.html: For each episode, record the total reward from the first time you reach a state to the end (first-visit), or from every time you're there (every-visit). Average over episodes. Both get there with enough data.

how.title: A tiny grid world
how.html: Four episodes in a row of five squares: exiting right pays +10, exiting left −10, each move −1. Averaging gives C = 4, B = 8, E = −2. Odd: B and E both lead to C, so why so different? Because MC only learns each square from the episodes that passed through it.

how.title: Keep a running average
how.html: No need to store every return: nudge the estimate by (new return − estimate)/count. Or nudge by a fixed fraction to adapt if things change.

how.title: From scoring to choosing
how.html: To choose actions without a model, score state–action pairs (Q), then always pick the highest. Repeat: score with new episodes, then improve. The same evaluate–improve loop as before, but learned from play.

how.title: Don't stop exploring
how.html: If you always pick the current favourite, you never learn about the other actions. Either start episodes from random situations (exploring starts) or keep a small chance ε of trying anything (ε-soft).

how.title: Learning from someone else's play
how.html: On-policy: learn about the strategy you're using. Off-policy: learn about a different (e.g. greedy) strategy from data generated by another one, reweighting each episode by how likely the target strategy was to act that way.

demo.html: Play thousands of blackjack hands and let Monte Carlo work out when to stick (S) or hit (H). Watch the familiar strategy emerge: stick on 17+, stick on 13–16 if the dealer shows a weak card.

example.html:
Averaging C. State C appears in all four episodes. Three times the agent went on to exit at +10 (return 9), once to exit at −10 (return −11). Average: (9 + 9 − 11 + 9)/4 = 4. With the running-average update the estimate goes 9, 9, 2.33, 4.

Supplementary MC needs episodes to end. For tasks that never end, or very long ones, TD learning (next sessions) updates as it goes.

misunderstandings: The return is only known at the end.
Shared successors give similar MC values.
Each state learns only from its own episodes.
ε-soft control finds the best deterministic policy.
It finds the best ε-soft policy.
takeaways: MC estimates values by averaging actual returns.
No model, no bootstrapping, but high variance and waits for episode ends.
Control uses Q and greedy improvement (GPI) with continued exploration.
Off-policy MC reweights returns by π/b.
thirty: Monte Carlo methods learn values from complete sampled episodes by averaging returns, with no model and no bootstrapping. First-visit MC averages the return after the first visit to a state per episode; every-visit averages all visits. In a five-state grid world four episodes give V = (−10, 8, 4, 10, −2) for A–E; B and E differ although both lead to C because MC learns each state in isolation. Updates can be incremental (1/N) or constant-α. MC control estimates Q and improves greedily (GPI), keeping exploration alive with exploring starts or ε-soft policies (converging to the best ε-soft policy). Off-policy MC learns a target policy from behaviour data using importance-sampling ratios (ordinary: unbiased, high variance; weighted: biased, low variance). Blackjack, easy to simulate but hard to model, is the classic example.
